# Response to Letter to the Editor

**Authors:** Melissa M. Chang; Christopher D. Yang; Huy Q. Ly; Ken Y. Lin

**Affiliations:** 1University of California, Irvine School of Medicine, Irvine, California, 92697 | 2Gavin Herbert Eye Institute, Department of Ophthalmology, UC Irvine, California, 92697 | 3Department of Biomedical Engineering, UC Irvine, California 92697

We appreciate the concerns that Dr. Parul Bansal and Dr. Julie Pegu have raised regarding our original manuscript “Anterior Chamber Washout During Ahmed Valve Glaucoma Surgery Reduces the Incidence of Hypertensive Phase”1. Below are our point-by-point responses:

- Firstly, we appreciate the authors’ efforts in conducting this study. However, we noticed a discrepancy in the definition of the hypertensive phase. The study defines it as intraocular pressure exceeding 21 mmHg within six months post-procedure on maximum tolerated medical therapy. In contrast, the standard definition defines the hypertensive phase as intraocular pressure exceeding 21 mmHg within three to six months of anti-glaucoma surgery, regardless of the use of anti-glaucoma medications (2). We would like to know the number of patients who experienced a hypertensive phase but were effectively controlled with antiglaucoma medications.We acknowledge the discrepancies in the various clinical descriptions of hypertensive phase. Concerns about these discrepancies are reasonable. However, our study question sought to assess whether intraoperative anterior chamber washout affected the odds of hypertensive phase in patients receiving maximum tolerated medical therapy postoperatively. If patients who experienced a hypertensive phase were effectively controlled with antiglaucoma medications, they would not have met criteria for study inclusion in the first place. That said, the point you raise is well taken, and it will make an excellent topic for a future study.

- Secondly, we observed that two patients with uveitic glaucoma were included in the study. Considering that uveitic glaucoma patients may already have elevated levels of proinflammatory cytokines, this inclusion might have introduced a bias in the analysis of results. It would be helpful to know if these patients were in the active phase of uveitis or in a remission phase.We acknowledge that the inclusion of patients with uveitic glaucoma may have biased regression analyses assessing pre-existing autoimmune comorbidities as predictors of hypertensive phase. The first patient with uveitis was in remission on a prednisolone taper. The second patient with uveitis was in an active phase in the context of steroid nonadherence. We contend that one would expect increased odds of hypertensive phase in these patients. Yet, we found that pre-existing diagnoses of autoimmune disease such as uveitis and type 1 diabetes mellitus did not significantly predict hypertensive phase.

- Furthermore, the surgical approach described in the study mentions the anterior placement of the Ahmed Glaucoma Valve Implant (FP7 model) by suturing it to the sclera with 8–0 Vicryl through the two anterior plate islets, 4–5 mm posterior to the limbus. The conventional practice, however, is to suture the FP7 implant 8–9 mm posterior to the limbus. We would appreciate clarification on the specific reasons for the anterior placement of the AGV, as anterior positioning may lead to early plate exposure and asthenopic symptoms.The authors acknowledge this mistake in our initial description of the surgical approach, and that the conventional practice of suturing the FP7 implant 8–9 mm posterior to the limbus was used instead. We apologize for any confusion.

- Moreover, the study reports postoperative intraocular pressure measurements in the anterior chamber washout and control groups at 1 week, 3 months, and 6 months postoperatively. Notably, only the reduction in intraocular pressure at 1 week postoperatively was found to be significant. As most of the eyes had very high IOP, this raises concerns about the potential complications associated with the sudden lowering of intraocular pressure, such as decompression retinopathy, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, and choroidal detachment. In neovascular glaucoma, anterior chamber washout may also lead to bleeding from fragile neovascular vessels (3).During glaucoma surgery, drastic changes in intraocular pressure can and often happen, usually as the entry into the eye is made. However, if there is hyphema, the treatment is anterior chamber washout. In our experience, if anterior washout is performed slowly, it does not cause bleeding, and definitely does not cause decompression retinopathy or suprachoroidal hemorrhage. These are rare risks associated not with anterior chamber washout but rather traditional glaucoma surgeries in general.

- Furthermore, the study’s minimum follow-up period was stated as 6 months. However, there are reports indicating an increase in intraocular pressure at 2 years of follow-up after surgery (4). This raises questions about the long-term maintenance of intraocular pressure within the same range for 5 out of 9 participants who received washout in this study. While this study presents an innovative approach to reducing the incidence of the hypertensive phase, the authors acknowledged their limitations. Evaluating the anterior chamber washout method in a larger population would be valuable to gain insight into its long-term effects.We appreciate the reports indicating an increase in intraocular pressure at the 2-year follow-up time point after Ahmed glaucoma valve surgery. However, most of these instances of hypertensive phase occur within the 6-month postoperative period. Future studies evaluating anterior chamber washout will benefit from assessing a larger population across a larger follow-up period.

## References
